I've been farming this same land for 20 years. I know this soil and I know what it needs. My farm is small — 2.6 mu — and it's all the same land, wheat in winter then maize in summer, like everyone around here. I don't have money to experiment. I have seven mouths and some kids away working, so I need a reliable harvest, not a gamble.

**My thinking on wheat:**
I'll plant in early October after the autumn rains. I'll buy improved seed from the township supply cooperative — the same kind I've used the last few years, a Jimai variety or whatever the co-op has that did well locally. I won't try something new. I'll do rotary tillage after the maize comes off, chop the stalks in, and sow. I'll apply compound fertilizer as a base before seeding, then topdress urea in early spring at green-up. Irrigation — I need at least three: one before winter to help the roots settle, one at jointing, one at heading. Maybe a fourth at grain fill if it's dry. I'll spray herbicide in late February or early March when the weeds are small, and probably one fungicide at heading to protect against rust — I lost yield to that a few years back.

**My thinking on maize:**
Right after the wheat comes off in June, I get the land ready fast and plant — delay costs me yield. I always buy hybrid seed, that's just what maize is now. I'll do light rotary tillage to turn in the wheat stubble. I apply base compound fertilizer at planting and topdress with urea at the jointing stage, that's when the crop needs it most. Summer rains help, but I'll irrigate once or twice — at emergence if it's dry, and at silking if needed. I spray herbicide right after planting while the weeds are small, and watch for corn borer; if I see damage I'll spray once.

I'm not going to change much from last year. What I do works well enough, and changing things on a small farm with no savings is risky.
